hook_text: Some of South Africa's diamonds travelled hundreds of kilometres to the sea, carried by a river.
clip_script: Deep underground, diamonds form under enormous pressure. Volcanic pipes bring them up near Kimberley, locked in rock. Then, for millions of years, the weather goes to work. Rain, heat and frost break the rock down where it lies. That is weathering. Next, rivers pick up the pieces, and the Orange River carries diamonds, sand and gravel towards the Atlantic. That is erosion. Where the river slows, it drops its heaviest load. At the coast, waves sort the gravel and drop the diamonds on beaches. That is deposition. Weathering breaks. Erosion takes. Deposition drops. The same three steps carve deep dongas into farmland, pile up the giant red dunes of the Namib, build beaches of quartz sand, and slowly fill our dams with mud. Mountains wear down. New land builds up. And the cycle never stops.
visual_style: A cut-away of a volcanic pipe with glittering diamonds; rock cracking in sun and frost; a winding brown river crossing a dry landscape to the ocean; waves rolling gravel on a beach; three words appearing: breaks, takes, drops.
pacing: A journey from underground to the sea, speeding up as the river flows.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn the difference between weathering, erosion and deposition.
